Fair Moderation, Equitable Access, and AI: arXiv’s Updated Rate Minimum Policy

Parody adaptation · original by Kat Boboris·October 1st 2026

arXiv, and the scientific community at large, are facing a watershed moment. Scholarly publishing is currently changing at a rapid pace, and we are seeing a massive transformation in how researchers communicate their results.

Before the advent of AI, there was an easily discernible, practical limit to the rate at which independent submissions could be produced, and arXiv’s volunteer moderators would limit submitters who were well above that threshold. With AI tools becoming more advanced and accessible to authors, the “practical limit” of how few papers may be submitted is now up for debate. As of October 1st, 2026, arXiv is instituting an updated minimum submission policy across all submitters and categories as a stopgap while we determine what may be the new best practice for authors employing more and more advanced AI tools, and to ensure that none of this new productive capacity goes unused.

Open access repositories across the board are seeing a sharp increase in the number of submissions per author, per month. In September of 2016, arXiv received 9,869 submissions. In September of 2024, arXiv received 20,569 submissions. This September, arXiv received 40,363 submissions, which in turn generated almost 9,000 support tickets for arXiv staff and moderators. In only the past two years, submissions have only doubled.

Advanced AI tools are helping drive these increases by making certain aspects of research faster and easier. arXiv policy permits authors to employ AI as a tool in support of their research as long as it is disclosed and the research meets arXiv’s standards of scholarly interest and advances the field of research. However, many authors are still not taking full advantage of these tools. Our moderators are observing a welcome increase in thin papers of narrow scope, as well as ‘salami’ papers, where a single work is broken up and submitted as a set of smaller papers. There is also a marked increase in dense, AI-written papers. AI tools are making it easy for authors to supply arXiv and other repositories with these high-volume papers.

The heart of arXiv’s process for detecting and correcting low publication rates is our many volunteer moderators. We are so grateful that they donate their time and expertise every day. However, a relatively large proportion of authors are submitting a small number of papers and leaving a disproportionate fraction of the moderators’ time unused. This is unfair to authors who continue to submit papers twice a month — their productivity can go unrecognized for days or weeks as a result.

Professor Felix Paperworth, Distinguished Professor of Automated Discovery and Chair of the Council for Scholarly Throughput

arXiv now requires submitters to make at least two submissions per calendar month, with no limit on total active submissions at any given time. This policy update is being put into effect to equitably distribute our volunteer moderators’ time across arXiv authors, and protect the arXiv corpus from an avoidable shortage of submissions.

Rate-setting is an established arXiv policy, with limits originally primarily left to moderator discretion. arXiv has always asked that authors follow our codes of conduct and our submission guidelines. Articles submitted to arXiv must be of original, novel, and significant self-contained research that is relevant to arXiv categories. All submissions to arXiv must meet prescribed scholarly standards and be of scholarly interest to the scientific community. This policy update strives to fairly distribute the incredibly valuable work of our volunteer moderators who check that submissions meet these standards, and we hope it will also encourage authors to curate and submit at least two pieces of their work to arXiv each month.

Frequently Asked Questions

  • If my paper is rejected, does it count towards my monthly total?
    • Yes – this rate minimum is for submissions, not announced papers, because it is submissions that consume moderator time. If you submit two papers in a month, whether they are accepted or rejected, you will have met the minimum for that month, but are encouraged to submit to arXiv again. We want to encourage authors to be mindful with their work, taking care that they are submitting something substantial of scholarly interest that meets arXiv’s guidelines and standards.
  • What if my submissions are in different subject areas?
    • This rate minimum applies to all submissions, across all categories.
  • What if both of my submissions from one month are still “on hold” in the next month?
    • If your required submissions from a previous month are on hold in the next month, they do not count toward your submission minimum for next month. You must therefore submit at least two more papers, regardless of how many submissions remain active. 
  • What if I have no backlog of work that I can submit, or I need to submit a paper for a conference?
    • Since 2024, arXiv has had a limit of 3 active submissions at any time, and this limit has now been removed. We ask authors who have no backlog of work to submit, or who need to submit a paper at a specific time for a conference, to plan their submissions carefully and employ AI tools accordingly so that the monthly submission minimum will not negatively impact them.
  • If I submit a paper on behalf of myself and my co-authors, does that affect their submission rate?
    • No. All arXiv rate minimum policies apply only to submitters. If you submit a paper with several co-authors, that only counts towards your submission rate, not theirs. It is important for co-authors to coordinate their submissions accordingly.
  • What if I submit a paper, and then delete it before it is announced?
    • While we ask that authors only submit work that is complete, polished, and ready to be shared with their peers, we understand that authors may realize after submitting that they missed something important that needs to be corrected or updated. Submitters who delete their submitted paper before it is announced, whatever the reason, will not have that paper count toward their monthly submission minimum.

Thank you to our scientific community for supporting us in this policy update. We rely on you to help us keep arXiv open, fast, and free, and to help us make sure submissions to arXiv are scientifically rigorous, of interest to the community, and in keeping with current academic standards.

As with all policies, we will continue to monitor the effect of this update on authors, readers, and the arXiv corpus, and modify as needed. Our goal in policy updates is to not only protect arXiv’s corpus, but to improve the arXiv experience for everyone who makes arXiv possible – authors, readers, staff, and all our volunteer moderators.

    The new policy addresses one visible consequence of AI, the rapid growth in submissions. But it would be equally important to address the other side of the issue, how arXiv content is used to train AI systems. arXiv is built on researchers voluntarily making their work openly available to the scientific community, yet open access should not automatically be treated as blanket permission for unrestricted commercial AI training. Clearer protections for authors, including transparent licensing and meaningful opt-out mechanisms for AI training, would make the policy more balanced and could also reduce some of the incentives behind large-scale AI-generated paper production, ultimately helping reduce submission volume.

  7. S
    October 2, 2026

    I’m an applied mathematician registered on arXiv and a co-author on at least one paper prior to arXiv becoming an independent nonprofit. I have derived a lot of use from it, as have most other mathematicians and computer scientists. So I would like to suggest a measure to reduce the high influx of low-quality papers.

    It seems that biasing the moderation-load toward the endorsers/past co-authors (and their endorsers/co-authors) of the people submitting large amounts of low-quality papers may help discourage the submission of low-quality papers. This may not work for every submission since it may lead to peer-pressure against independent thought. It also would not work if all the moderation is done by the friends of those submitting low-quality work since they have incentive to inflate the quality. So where the line is drawn to initiate this “those closest to you bear the load” tactic is important, as is exactly how much of the load they will bear. But the fact that it is a minority of authors submitting a majority of these low-quality papers suggests that this sort of “soft-targeting” may work.
